[prose] Understanding species adaptations to human-modified ecosystems is central to evolutionary and conservation biology. It is essential to evaluate trait variations in populations that occur along environmental gradients to understand the adaptive potential of species to human-driven environmental change. We analyzed morphological trait variations in the workers of four common and phylogenetically distant ant species (Dinoponera quadriceps, Dorymyrmex goeldii, Pheidole radoszkowskii, and Ectatomma muticum) along disturbance and aridity gradients in the Caatinga dry forest. Ants were collected using pitfall traps in 20 0.1-ha plots distributed over an area of 213.75 km 2 . Up to five individuals per species were selected from each plot to measure eight morphological traits. Between-plot variability contributed considerably (\~37%) to the total variability of morphological traits. This pattern of high between-plot variability was consistent across species and traits. Such morphological intraspecific variations between plots were not strongly related to the aridity or disturbance gradients. However, when ant morphology did respond to environmental change, the response was stronger to aridity rather than disturbance, and responses were most conspicuous in P. radoskowskii. Our results suggest that ants in the Caatinga may have substantial potential for morphological adaptation to environmental changes and that disturbance intensity and variations in aridity are not strong determinants of ant worker morphology despite influencing morphological variation over small geographical distances. These morphological variations are likely to represent key assets, by enabling individuals and population to inhabit the variety of habitats provided by Caatinga and to cope with upcoming changes in land use and climate.

[prose] Intraspecific variability within plots made the largest contribution to total variation for most morphological traits and species, but intraspecific variation between plots was considerable (Figure 1). The mean (±SE) contribution of between-plot variability to total variability was $3 7 \pm 3 \%$ (range: 16.7–85.6%) and did not differ among species $( \mathsf { A N O V A } ; F _ { 3 , 2 7 } = 0 . 2 , p = 0 . 8 6 1 )$ or morphological traits (ANOVA; $F _ { 7 , 2 3 } = 1 . 9 , p = 0 . 1 3 0 )$ . The lowest values of between-plot variability ( 70%) were for clypeus length ratio in E. muticum and D. quadriceps (Figure 1). In general, most traits were not correlated with each other, and when they were, most were not highly correlated (i.e., $r 0 . 7 0 )$ in both species. P. radoskowiskii was the ant species with fewest traits significantly correlated with each other (6 out of 28), and none of the correlation coefficients were greater than 0.70. For D. goeldii, out of the 21 possible correlation coefficients, six were significant and none of them were greater than 0.70 (Figure S3).

[prose] 28 million people who are highly dependent on forest natural re sources for their livelihoods in a typical regime of chronic anthropogenic disturbance (Silva et al., 2017). In addition, Caatinga is highly threatened by climate change, with climate models forecasting a 22–40% reduction in rainfall and a 3–6°C increase in temperatures by 2100 (Magrin et al., 2014). Increasing aridity has been observed even within small geographic ranges (Rito et al., 2017). Thus, Caatinga offers an excellent opportunity to study potential morphological adaptations to disturbance and climate change. Moreover, previous research on the Caatinga has shown that chronic anthropogenic disturbance and/or aridity do not affect ant abundance or species richness, but does alter species composition (Arnan, Arcoverde, et al., 2018; Câmara et al., 2018; Oliveira et al., 2017) and spatial–temporal foraging activity of widely distributed species (Silva et al., 2019). Despite this, many species are unaffected and occur along a large portion of the disturbance and/or aridity gradients. Morphological traits may play an important role in how ant populations respond to increases in chronic disturbance and aridity gradients.

[prose] Our specific aims are: (1) to characterize and quantify the levels of morphological intraspecific variation within and between study plots throughout the region, (2) to verify to what extent morphological intraspecific variation depends on species or morphological trait identity, and (3) to test to what extent morphological intraspecific variation responds to changes in disturbance and aridity. We pre-dict that: (1) the degree of morphological intraspecific variation will depend on species or morphological trait identity, as previous studies have suggested that some ant clades exhibit greater trait conservatism than others (Hölldobler & Wilson, 1990; Silva & Brandão, 2010; Weiser & Kaspari, 2006), and some traits tend to be more plastic than others (Gaudard et al., 2019; Oms et al., 2017; Purcell et al., 2016; Yates et al., 2014); and (2) morphological intraspecific variation will respond to changes in disturbance and aridity, as they are the strongest environmental filters in the study area (Arnan, Arcoverde, et al., 2018; Rito et al., 2017).

[prose] were activated for 48 h in March 2015 (for more details on ant sampling, see Arnan, Arcoverde, et al., 2018). We selected the four most widely distributed species (i.e., species occurring in ≥10 plots) in our study landscape to measure morphological attributes, which belonged to four different subfamilies following an evolutionary gradient from the closest to the baseline to the most evolutionary recent species (Dinoponera quadriceps (Ponerinae), Dorymyrmex goeldii (Dolichoderinae), Pheidole radoszkowskii (Myrmicinae), and Ectatomma muticum (Ectatomminae)) (Moreau & Bell, 2013). These species also follow a gradient of worker size, with D. quadriceps displaying the largest workers, P. radoskowskii the smallest workers, and E. muticum and D. goeldii exhibiting intermediate sized workers. For each species and plot, we measured between 3 and 10 (median = 5) randomly selected workers from the captured individuals. A recent study showed that, on average, measuring around six individual worker ants is enough to generate a trait mean close to the population mean (Gaudard et al., 2019). Moreover, many studies and databases of ant traits use between three and 10 individuals (Bishop et al., 2015; Gibb et al., 2014; Parr et al., 2017; Silva & Brandão, 2010). Out of the 20 plots, we could only collect between 3 and 5 individuals in 14 plots for D. quadriceps, 13 plots for E. muticum and P. radoszkowskii, and 10 plots for D. goeldii. The plots where each species occurred were well distributed along both our chronic anthropogenic disturbance and aridity gradients, except for Dormyrmex goeldii that only occurred in the most arid plots (Figure S2).
